extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent agents/attorneys, and examiners working on biotechnology/sequence/antibody applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and examination standards for preparing and prosecuting patent applications involving nucleotide/amino acid sequence listings, biological deposits, and antibody-related claims, including representation, corrections, sufficiency, anticipation, and enablement considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion and numbering of sequences in sequence listing
rubrics_metrics.description: Each nucleotide or amino acid sequence disclosed in the specification, other than a sequence identified as forming a part of the prior art, must be included in a sequence listing. Each sequence in the sequence listing is assigned a sequence identification number, which is a unique number (integer). The numbers must begin with number 1 and increase in sequential order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a sequence identification number has no sequence (an intentionally skipped sequence), use "000" in place of a sequence. Except where the entire sequence listing is removed, the original sequence identification number for a given sequence should be maintained after amendment; when a sequence is removed it must be replaced with "000" and any references in the specification to that sequence identification number should also be deleted. The total number of all sequences must be indicated (SequenceTotalQuantity) and must equal the total number of sequence identification numbers including intentionally skipped sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of sequences elsewhere in the application
rubrics_metrics.description: If a sequence included in a sequence listing is referred to in the claims, the drawings or the part of the description other than the sequence listing, the reference must include the sequence identification number preceded by "SEQ ID NO:" in accordance with subsection 58(4) of the Patent Rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example provided where failure to identify a referenced sequence as SEQ ID NO:9 was identified as a defect. Always use the exact prefix format "(SEQ ID NO:X)" when cross-referencing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ambiguity/variable symbols ('n' and 'X')
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambiguity symbols "n" (nucleotide) and "X" (amino acid) can be used to define residues that are unknown, modified, abasic or a variant; these symbols can represent only a single residue at a specific position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "n" has default value any one of "a","c","g","t/u"; "X" has a specified default set of amino acids. If "n" or "X" represents something other than the default value, the corresponding nucleotide or amino acid must be further annotated in the feature table for that sequence. For variable-length sequences, present enough discrete symbols to represent the maximum length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of modified nucleotides and amino acids
rubrics_metrics.description: Modified nucleotides and amino acids should, whenever possible, be represented as the corresponding unmodified residues; where they cannot be represented by another symbol, use "n" or "X" and further describe them in the feature table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 4-acetylcytidine represented by "n" and annotated with "ac4c" in the feature table; 2-aminoadipic acid represented by "X" and annotated "Aad". See PCT Sequence Listing Standard Annex tables for symbols and abbreviations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of sequence variants and required sequence features
rubrics_metrics.description: Sequence variants (alternatives, deletions, insertions, substitutions) are to be represented in the sequence listing per the PCT standard. The PCT Sequence Listing Standard requires identification in the sequence listing of certain features, if present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required features (if present) include nucleotide analogues (e.g., PNAs), D-amino acids, abasic sites, and linear regions of a branched sequence when the region contains 10 or more specifically-defined nucleotides or 4 or more specifically-defined amino acids. Consult the PCT standard for paragraph references and detailed representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner consideration of sequence nomenclature vs statutory clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of the foregoing symbols and nomenclature relates to how sequences are represented, but during examination an examiner must consider whether such use contravenes the Patent Act and/or Rules (for example on the basis of clarity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nomenclature compliance does not automatically satisfy statutory clarity requirements; examiners assess clarity under chapter references (e.g., 23.05.01).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction of a sequence listing
rubrics_metrics.description: Corrections to a sequence listing found to contain errors must comply with the requirements of section 38.2 of the Patent Act: no new matter may be added and any correction must be reasonably inferable from the specification or drawings as filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions/special rules apply for divisional applications and applications originally filed in a language other than English or French. Corrections that require new experimental data (e.g., re-sequencing) are not reasonably inferable and thus are not allowable corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory requirements for deposits of biological material
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a specification refers to a deposit of biological material and the deposit is in accordance with the regulations, the deposit shall be considered part of the specification and may be taken into consideration in determining compliance with subsection 27(3). Sections 93 to 98 of the Patent Rules regulate deposits of biological material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paragraph 93(1)(a): deposit must be made by the applicant or predecessor with an international depositary authority (IDA) on or before the filing date. Before public inspection, the applicant must inform the Commissioner of the name of the IDA and the accession number (paragraph 93(1)(b)), and the description must include this information to satisfy paragraph 93(1)(c). Examiners may requisition the applicant to amend the description to include the deposit date where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposits' evidentiary role vs presumption of necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference to a deposit in a specification does not create a presumption that the deposit is required to comply with subsection 27(3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deposits are taken into consideration where appropriate, but the mere fact a deposit was made does not automatically mean the invention has been adequately described for patentability purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of disclosure when a deposit is relied upon
rubrics_metrics.description: If an invention cannot be enabled without access to a biological material, a deposit of that material may be necessary to make the description sufficient under subsection 27(3), unless the required material is publicly known and reliably available to the person skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A biological material is 'reliably available' if it can be obtained commercially or reproducibly prepared/isolated using established procedures without undue experimentation. For plant seeds, reliable availability means enabling one to obtain a reproducible homogeneous population identical to the plant of the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposit does not substitute for full description when product can be defined
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that a biological deposit has been made does not of itself mean an invention has been adequately described; a claim to a desired product does not merit protection simply because reference is made to where the product can be found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the product can be defined in clear and explicit terms (e.g., DNA sequence), a deposit is not a substitute for a full and correct description. Whenever possible, include both deposit information and a clear explicit description of the product or method of making it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation considerations for prior art requiring biological material
rubrics_metrics.description: If a prior art disclosure requires access to a biological material in order for the matter described to be practised, the biological material must necessarily have been reliably available to the person skilled in the art before the claim date in order for that prior art disclosure to be anticipatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate that a prior art document disclosing a strain without a deposit may be non-enabling (and thus non-anticipatory) if the strain was not reliably available. Conversely, if prior art enables construction/isolation by known methods from publicly available elements, the claim can be anticipated even without a deposit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antibody claim characterization: generic vs particular
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim to 'an antibody which specifically binds to antigen X' typically represents a generic group of structurally different antibodies sharing binding specificity. A claim defined by nucleotide/amino acid sequences or by reference to a deposited hybridoma encompasses only the particular antibody.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between genus-style functional antibody claims (broad) and structurally-defined or deposit-defined claims (narrow); the scope affects support and enablement requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: General support and enablement requirements for antibody claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim to an antibody must be supported by a specification that correctly and fully describes the antibody invention and its operation/use and must set out clearly the steps in a process or method of making/using the antibody in full, clear, concise and exact terms so as to enable any person skilled in the art to make or use it (subsection 27(3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification must enable and correctly/fully describe the invention as of the filing date. Claims must also distinctly and explicitly define novel, non-obvious, useful, and statutory subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for generic antibody claims (antigen characterization/antiserum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, a claim to an antibody specific for antigen X will be considered supported if antigen X itself has been fully characterized and either antiserum has been prepared, or if antiserum has not been prepared there is no indication that producing such an antibody would be unlikely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A fully characterized antigen (e.g., complete amino acid sequence for a protein) can serve as a correct and full description of corresponding polyclonal antibodies; other characterizations (formula, chemical name, properties, deposit) may also be adequate if they allow skilled persons to understand the scope of the antibody claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polyclonal antibody disclosure expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Polyclonal antibodies are treated as a generic group representing the family of antibodies in antiserum capable of binding a target antigen; methods for preparing polyclonal sera are well known and a specification generally does not need to describe them in detail to be enabling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the antigen sufficiently (sequence, properties, deposit) so that the person skilled in the art understands the scope of the claim. If antigen X is known/obvious in prior art, polyclonal antibodies reactive with it are generally obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monoclonal antibody enablement factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Enablement for monoclonal antibody claims is fact-specific. Examiners should consider factors including: whether the applicant actually prepared a monoclonal antibody; where not prepared, whether the target antigen was fully characterized; availability/ease of antigen production; absence of indications the applicant/others were unable to produce the antibody; absence of indications undue experimentation would be necessary; and whether the scope of the antibody claim is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a person skilled in the art, given common general knowledge and only the specification and the fully characterized antigen, would be enabled to produce the monoclonal antibody without inventive ingenuity or undue experimentation, enablement is satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monoclonal antibody correct and full description factors
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification must provide a correct and full description of a monoclonal antibody invention. Consider whether the antigen was fully characterized; if not, whether the applicant prepared and characterized the monoclonal antibody; whether a hybridoma producing the antibody was deposited in accordance with the Patent Rules on or before the filing date; and whether the scope of the antibody claim with respect to the antigen is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paragraph 27(3)(a) may be satisfied by describing the fully characterized antigen to which the monoclonal antibody specifically binds, but depending on facts, a disclosure of a representative antibody embodiment, deposit, or explicit sequences of binding regions may be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: When detailed support is required for monoclonal antibody claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed support beyond a simple binding claim may be required where the applicant asserts functional properties beyond mere binding (agonist/antagonist/neutralizing activity), specificity for a particular epitope, remarkably high affinity, where the antigen is complex, or where there are indications antibodies to the class are difficult to raise or cross-reactivity/obviousness concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed support can take the form of a representative antibody embodiment, a biological deposit (e.g., hybridoma), or explicit disclosure of amino acid sequences of binding regions, epitopes, or binding pockets essential to function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements specific to antibody inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to enablement and description, a claimed monoclonal antibody must be novel, non-obvious, and useful under sections 28.2, 28.3 and section 2 of the Patent Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty and inventive step may be supported by novel/ inventive antigen characterization; claims may be made more particular (and thus more likely novel/non-obvious) by reciting structure (nucleotide/amino acid sequences), reference to a deposited hybridoma, or a specific and supported binding activity such as higher-than-expected affinity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for claims to nucleic acids or polypeptides relating to antibodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an application claims nucleic acids or polypeptides relating to antibodies (e.g., light/heavy chains, variable regions, CDRs), the nucleic acids and polypeptides must be fully supported by the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the general sequence disclosure rules (see chapter 23.05) to ensure adequate support for sequence-based claims.
